question: In a claims-processing screen, the code calls repository.save(claim) immediately after every property change, and opens a database transaction when the user starts and keeps it open across several HTTP requests. What problems does Fowler identify with this, and how would a Unit of Work change the design?

cases.answer: Saving on every change produces lots of very small database calls, which is slow: change one object at three points and you get three calls instead of one with its final state. Keeping a transaction open for the whole interaction is impractical when the business transaction spans multiple requests. A Unit of Work keeps track of everything you do during a business transaction that can affect the database: new objects to insert, dirty objects to update, removed objects to delete, and objects read if you need to check for inconsistent reads. At commit it works out everything that needs to change and writes it out, so the system transaction only needs to be open at the end. Its strength is keeping all this in one place instead of tracking changes in variables or by walking dirty flags, which is hard with a Domain Model's object graph. It is also the platform for business transactions that span several system transactions, using Optimistic or Pessimistic Offline Lock.
must_credit: many small DB calls are slow
long-open transaction across requests is impractical
tracks new/dirty/removed objects; writes all at commit
keeps change tracking in one place; works with offline locks

cases.answer: A Unit of Work keeps a list of the objects you've changed and saves them all at the end in one go instead of saving each time.
must_credit: inserts and deletes (not only changes) are missing

cases.answer:
Saving after every change means many tiny database calls, which is slow, and holding a transaction open across several requests is impractical for a business transaction that spans them. A Unit of Work tracks new, dirty and deleted objects during the business transaction and writes everything out at commit, so the system transaction only opens at the end. It keeps change tracking in one place, which is much easier than variables or dirty flags in a Domain Model, and it's the base for offline locking across system transactions.
